results.description:
You've checked the boxes. The day still didn't happen.

Routinery tracks your routines and then runs them with you.

App of the Day 2026 (Apple) - Best ADHD App of 2025 (Forbes Health) - 5 million downloads

A habit tracker, routine tracker and day planner in one. Stack small habits into a daily routine, break it into 1-5 minute steps, and each step runs on its own timer while a voice calls out what comes next.

Morning routines, bedtime wind-downs, study blocks, workouts, medication - anything with a fixed order runs the same way.

WHY IT WORKS
- Starting gets easier. "Study" is too big to begin; "sit at the desk, 1 min" is not. Small steps lower the cost of the first move.
- Nothing to decide mid-run. You set the order once, when you built the routine. Nothing left to choose means less to stall on.
- Wins come back often. A finish is logged every step, not once a day.
- No time math. You set each step's length once. Sink into one thing and the voice pulls you out, so an afternoon doesn't vanish.

ASK CHATGPT OR CLAUDE TO BUILD IT
- "Make me a 40-minute weekday morning routine" and it lands in the app.
- Your assistant can handle routines alongside other tools you've connected there, like Google Calendar.
- Connects to ChatGPT, Claude and others over our MCP server, included in the free plan.

IT STARTS ON TIME, SCREEN OR NOT
- Set the weekdays and time; the reminder arrives then. Weekdays only, three times a week, whatever your schedule.
- The voice reads each step aloud, so the routine keeps running while you shower or cook.
- A home screen widget shows today's list without opening the app.
- Start on the phone, carry on from watch, tablet, or Mac.

STAY DEEP IN ONE THING
- A pomodoro that announces the next task, so the block keeps its own momentum.
- Build the environment: white noise, Focus mode, landscape view, Shortcuts.
- Stretch a timer, skip a step, reorder what's left - all without leaving the run.

DON'T DO IT ALONE
- Share a routine's task list with family or a friend and see how far each of you got.
- Finish a routine and the result goes straight to the person you picked.

SEE IT ADD UP
- A plant grows for each day you keep a streak; weekly and monthly stats show what holds.

FOR THE DAILY AND THE ONE-OFF
- Keep undated tasks and weekly repeats in one daily routine planner.
- A one-time task gets a timer too.
- Can't face it now? Park it in Anytime for later.
- Shift work that moves weekly still fits: Morning, Afternoon, Evening.
- See the day as a list, a calendar, or a timeline.

WHO USES ROUTINERY
- Adults with ADHD who know the task and still can't start
- People who lose hours once they sink into something
- People who double-check in case they missed one
- Anyone who waits to start until they can do it perfectly
- Shift workers, people on daily medication, parents on the school run
- Anyone who wrote a routine down and never once ran it

ROUTINERY AT A GLANCE

Is Routinery free?
Yes. 2 routines free, no account, first one running in under a minute. Premium lifts the routine cap: monthly, 6-month or yearly. The free plan shows ads; Premium is ad-free.

Do I need an account, and what about privacy?
No account, no sign-up. Routine data is stored on our servers; usage analytics go through third-party tools. What you type is never used to train AI models. Email hello@routinery.app and we delete your data.

Does Routinery work offline?
Almost entirely. Routines, timers, voice, reminders and history run offline. Only device sync needs a connection.

What does Routinery connect to?
Siri Shortcuts, widgets, Apple Watch, and AI assistants over MCP. No direct sync with Apple Health or calendars. No export button either; pull your data out over MCP instead, free plan included.

What devices does Routinery run on?
iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch. No web version.

Questions, bugs or ideas: hello@routinery.app

Routinery is not a medical device and does not diagnose or treat ADHD.

results.description:
It's 7:40. One sock on, breakfast going cold, and you've said "shoes" three times.

The first time was cheerful. The second had their name in it. The third sounded like someone you never planned to be.

Your child is not being difficult. They know every step of this morning and could recite it back to you. Knowing it has never been the problem.

The problem is that the order lives in your head. You hold the sequence, you call the next step, you supply the urgency. You are not reminding your child. You are being the routine.

Star Reward Charts is a reward chart with the order built in. Something you point at together, instead of something you recite.

Your child's morning becomes a short path on the screen. Make bed, breakfast, teeth, shoes, in your family's order. The step they are on is lit up, the rest wait behind it, and they press and hold to collect their own star as each one is done.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Start with the part you dread
Pick a routine, use the guided suggestions or add your own steps, then put them in your family's order.

2. Choose how each child sees it
A rainbow path suits a six-year-old and insults a twelve-year-old, who still needs the routine. So there are five views of the same routine, from the winding path to a plain list, saved per child. The look ages out years before the need does.

3. They collect their own stars
Your child presses and holds to collect a star for a finished step. The path brightens and the next step becomes current. No approval queue, no waiting on you. And if real life happens out of order, they can still collect a later star.

4. Finish and celebrate
Completing the routine opens the treasure chest and earns gems for monster items. Stars build towards a real reward your family chose together: ice cream, the park, a toy, picking the film on Friday. That part is entirely yours.

YOU STAY IN CHARGE

- Give each routine its own steps, days, and optional reminder
- Anytime tasks keep extra jobs separate from the routine itself
- Adjust a balance, or undo a star or a reward claim, from history
- Share one iPhone, or use the same account on separate parent iPhones
- Child Mode hides parent screens and sets what each child can do
- No ads

THE ROUTINE COMES FIRST

The monster, the chest, and the gems celebrate progress. They are not the point. There is no pet to feed, no world to maintain, nothing that keeps your child in the app once the real routine is done. The chest opens because the bed got made. Then the app gets out of the way.

WHEN GETTING STARTED IS THE HARD PART

Some children stall at the start of a step, lose the thread halfway, or finish one thing with no idea what follows. Visible, ordered sequences are a familiar tool in those households, including families supporting autistic children.

If ADHD is part of your picture, the useful thing is not another reminder. It is the routine living on the screen instead of in your voice.
That is the whole design.

WHY I BUILT IT

I'm Paul, and I have ADHD. The part of me that was supposed to keep my daughter's chore chart going is the same part that loses the car keys.

I made her a paper chart. It lasted one school week. In week two I forgot to print a fresh one, and it sat on the fridge out of date while I gave the same instructions I'd always given.
What I wanted was the real routine on a screen, in order, with stars my daughters could collect themselves, because I am not reliable enough to be a dependency in my own family's morning.

And I'm still here. If something breaks, or you can't work out how to do something, you get me, not a ticketing system.

The first hour is not a to-do list.

Puttering is the old word for it: newspapers, breakfast, and nothing that has to be decided before ten. Most morning routine apps do the opposite and wake you into a scoreboard. Putter is a calm morning with a clock on it.

Pick 15, 30, 45 or 60 minutes and start. Your phone turns into:

• A warm, low-contrast clock you can read from across the kitchen. No second hand.
• A countdown you can't watch tick. It says "about 20 minutes left" and only changes when that stops being true.
• One plain place to put a thought if one shows up. No headings, no checkboxes, no tags.
• A slow ring under the clock, paced for box breathing if you feel like following it. Nothing tells you to.

What the app does that a browser can't:

• The sunrise. Over the last few minutes the screen warms up and the backlight itself comes up, so the room tells you it's nearly over. Your own brightness comes back the moment the buffer ends or you leave the app.
• Your note, handed back. When the buffer ends, anything you wrote is offered back so you can send it wherever you keep things. It stays in the pad either way.
• Clock mode. The same warm screen with no timer and nothing counted, and the screen stays on until you close it.

One thing it can't do on iPhone
iPhone doesn't let an app turn on Do Not Disturb or a Focus, so Putter doesn't pretend to. When a buffer starts it says so, and points you to Control Center if you want the phone quiet too.

One number
Consecutive mornings you didn't get pulled away. Finish the buffer and one a day counts. Locking the phone and setting it down is fine, as long as it has a passcode. Going off into another app for more than 45 seconds means that morning won't count. Miss a day and it starts again at one. No badges and no streak-loss guilt.

What it doesn't have, on purpose
• No account and no sign-in.
• No ads and no subscription. You pay once.
• No reminders and no congratulations. Putter never makes a sound.
• No internet connection. Putter doesn't connect to anything, so the only way a note leaves your phone is if you send it.

Putter isn't a treatment for anything and doesn't claim to do anything to your brain. It's an hour with a clock on it.

The morning sets the tone.

I've believed this for as long as I can remember. If I don't start my morning right, I tend to feel unproductive, restless, and scatter-brained throughout the rest of the day. So I've always put heavy emphasis on getting my mornings right.

But doing so was way harder than it should've been — my main problems being consistency (completing all the steps in the routine each day) and a lack of structure (without a basis for how long each part should take, it always felt like I was moving through routines instead of actually being in them).

Naturally, I turned to the plethora of morning routine apps on the App Store, but none of them really stuck. They were all cluttered, feature-heavy, and packed with metrics, streaks, and reminders — which felt like the opposite of what a morning should feel like. And underneath the noise, something more subtle was off: I never really felt like the morning was mine. These apps were focused on the act of building a routine — adding habits, checking boxes, hitting goals.

But I don't think of my morning as a routine. I think of it as a ritual. Checking the weather. A quote to sit with. Words of positivity left from days prior. A breath before the day begins.

That's what I wanted, and I couldn't find it. So I built it.

Daybreak is a doorway, not a dashboard.

Most morning apps are control panels — stacks of widgets, metrics, streaks, and reminders that demand your attention before you've even had water. Daybreak is the opposite. It's the small, quiet thing you pass through on the way into your day.

You design your morning. Daybreak walks you through it.

The whole point is to be less — less to manage, less to look at, less standing between you and the morning you actually want.

A ritual, not a routine. A doorway, not a dashboard.
